food.text: Maize was domesticated from a wild grass called teosinte, and it marked the shift from hunter-gatherers to farming and settled life in Mesoamerica. A single cob of maize could produce much more food than a cob of teosinte.

Squash, maize and beans, later grown together as the Three Sisters, all began in Mesoamerica. Squash was domesticated first, about 10,000 years ago, followed by maize and then beans. The whole process of developing this farming knowledge took 5,000 to 6,500 years.
Indigenous peoples of Mexico began to selectively breed maize plants around 8000 BC. This was the start of a crop that would become the centre of Mesoamerican farming and food.

Mesoamerica's Archaic period began around 8000 BCE and is known for the domestication of major crops, the development of agriculture and the beginning of sedentism. These changes let people move from hunting and gathering toward settled life, and they allowed complex societies to rise in the region.

In Mesoamerica, avocados, beans, chili peppers, gourds and squashes were grown from about 7000 BC. Around 4000 BC maize began to be grown, and soon after this tomatoes, so these crops were already familiar when the Bronze Age began.

The earliest known evidence of Cucurbita domestication is at least 8,000 years old. It was found in C. pepo samples from the Guilá Naquitz cave in Oaxaca, Mexico. It predates the domestication of maize and beans in the region by around 4,000 years.

Paleoecological evidence shows that maize and other crops were grown by slash-and-burn agriculture as early as 7300 BCE in the Central Balsas region and on the Caribbean coast of Mexico. Rising charcoal levels, falling tree pollen and rising maize pollen reveal the forest clearing.

During the Coxcatlán phase of the Middle Archaic Period, between 5700 and 3825 BC, the domestication of plants such as the chile is thought to have begun. Chiles became a relied-on source of food and were combined with maize, beans and squash.

The earliest horticulture was probably "dooryard horticulture", in which Archaic peoples nurtured a variety of plant species in small plots near where they lived. As agriculture intensified, they turned to slash-and-burn farming to clear larger areas further from home.

Early maize was not an easy crop to invest in. People mostly ate its unripened kernels, and before they settled into villages the output of wild maize did not justify the time and work needed to grow it.

Across Northern Belize, paleoecological evidence indicates that people began cultivating maize and manioc before 3000 BCE. Cassava-type root crops were therefore farmed alongside maize very early in the Maya region.

Silver-seeded gourds are grown for their seeds, which are rich in carbohydrates and fatty acids. Genomic evidence suggests they were domesticated at least 8,700 years ago, making them another very early Mesoamerican food plant.

Domesticating C. pepo squash changed the plant in measurable ways: larger seeds, thicker and sturdier peduncles, and a thicker rind. By about 8,000 years ago, samples had peduncles over 14mm across, unlike their wild ancestors.

Before maize was domesticated and became a main crop, it was used as the basis for beer. The beer was carried in decorated vessels and ceramic pottery to social and ritual occasions. At maize-linked ritual events and festivals, such as ball games, feasts and calendar turnings, royal members took part in the sacrifice of blood-letting and piercing, as repayment to the gods for giving the people maize that year.

art.text: Studies of cave and rock art from caves across Mexico, including regions near Guilá Naquitz in Oaxaca, show depictions of deer, sheep and bison, among other animals. Scholars take this as a sign that people still relied partly on hunted animals for food.
Farmers were present in the Maya lowlands by about 3000 BC. Along with the slow growth of agriculture, basic forms of pottery began to appear, with simple designs and some slipped vessels.

Mesoamerica's Archaic period, also called the Preceramic period, began around 8000 BCE and ended around 2000 BCE. Scholars find it unclear exactly when it gave way to the Preclassic, but the appearance of pottery, large-scale agriculture and villages signals the transition.

The Ortoiroid people were early settlers of the Caribbean, with a radiocarbon date of 5230 BC from Trinidad. They had no ceramics, but they wore jewelry made from perforated animal teeth. Their craft work also included bone spearpoints.

Zohapilco had a high population and was a clay-rich source for brickmaking. Its ceramic figurines could have influenced later Olmec civilization, and Olmec art shows that they could have adopted very similar styles.

In the Tehuacán Valley, archaeologist MacNeish found that a Late Archaic complex of stone bowls came before Mexico's first pottery. The first ceramics were monochrome wares named for Purrón Cave. They resembled the stone bowls and briefly existed alongside them.

Among the items found at Coxcatlan Cave in the Tehuacán Valley were an ink pen and containing vessels made using pre-ceramic material. The cave's domesticated plants date to between 5,000 and 3,400 BC, a time when no pottery was yet in use.

science.text: Squash was domesticated in Mesoamerica long before maize and beans. The earliest known evidence of Cucurbita domestication dates back at least 8,000 years, about 4,000 years before those crops, and comes from the Guilá Naquitz cave in Oaxaca, Mexico.

Archaic peoples cleared forest with slash-and-burn agriculture, using chipped stone adzes to cut down trees and dig. Paleoecological evidence, including more charcoal, less tree pollen and more maize pollen, shows maize was grown this way as early as 7300 BCE in the Central Balsas region and on the Caribbean coast of Mexico.

Early farmers changed the squash they grew. In Cucurbita pepo, domestication produced bigger seeds, thicker and sturdier peduncles (the stalks holding the fruit) and a thicker rind. By about 8,000 years ago the peduncles were more than 14mm across, unlike those of wild ancestors.

Maize could be dried and stored, which mattered greatly to early Mesoamericans because it could be used all year and carried elsewhere. It was often grown with the common bean, and the two plants provide complementary dietary amino acids.

The Ortoiroid were known for their lithic technology. Their stone tools included manos and metates, net sinkers, pestles, choppers, hammerstones and grinding pebbles. They made these without ceramics at sites such as Banwari Trace in Trinidad, which dates back at least to 5500 BC.

Genomic evidence suggests that the silver-seeded gourd, Cucurbita argyrosperma, was domesticated at least 8,700 years ago. It is commonly grown for its seeds, which are rich in carbohydrates and fatty acids.
Mesoamerican peoples discovered a way to improve the bioavailability of maize using a special process involving limewater. The process also added calcium to the food.

By 3500 BCE, Mesoamerican communities also exploited cotton, yucca and agave for fibers and textile materials. Around the same time, the common bean, tepary bean, scarlet runner bean, jicama, tomato and squash all became common cultivates.

Evidence of widespread forest clearing appears at different times across Mesoamerica. It starts around 5200 BCE on the Gulf coast and around 3500 BCE in the Maya Lowlands. In northern Belize, people cultivated maize and manioc before 3000 BCE, but widespread clearance only began after 2400 BCE.

culture.text: Beginning as early as 7000 BCE, people in Mesoamerica domesticated cacao, maize, beans, tomato, avocado, vanilla, squash and chili. They also domesticated the turkey and the dog. These changes reshaped daily life across the region.
Indigenous peoples of Mexico began to selectively breed maize plants around 8000 BC. This early crop breeding marks the start of the long farming tradition that later fed Mesoamerican civilizations.
By roughly 6000 BCE, hunter-gatherers in the highlands and lowlands of Mesoamerica began to develop agricultural practices. Their early cultivation focused on squash and chili.

By 3500 BCE, semi-agrarian communities across Mesoamerica commonly grew maize, common beans, tepary beans, scarlet runner beans, jicama, tomato and squash. Maize was the most common of these domesticated crops.

Around 3500 BCE, Mesoamerican farming communities did not only grow food. They also exploited cotton, yucca and agave for fibers and textile materials, which supplied the raw materials for cloth and cordage.

Northwestern Cuba is the only significant Gulf coast not connected to mainland North America, so it was inhabited millennia later than other regions. Its earliest known site of human habitation is Levisa, dated to 3100 BC.

The Lithic stage, or Paleo-Indian period, is the era of the first human habitation in Mesoamerica before agriculture and pottery. Its end point is commonly dated to about 8000 BCE, and the move to the following Archaic period is not a well-defined one.
